items.title: Testing
items.text: Every package is tested without network access, real clusters or real credentials. Interfaces at the package boundaries (agent.Model, agent.Approver, the model client, the SSH directory, the store path) let tests substitute in-process fakes.

items.title: Running tests
items.text:
make check                        # gofmt, go vet, go test ./..., cross-compile for Windows and macOS
go test ./...                     # all tests
go test ./internal/skill          # one package
go test ./internal/skill -run TestLoad     # tests whose name matches the regex
go test -race ./...               # with the race detector
go test -count=1 ./internal/store # bypass the test cache

make check is the gate for every commit. Run go test -race for any change that touches goroutines or the store, since the store is meant to be used by several processes at once.

items.title: How tests are organized
items.text:
Tests sit next to the code in *_test.go files. Files named review_test.go hold regression tests added after code review.

  • No network. The broker tests start an httptest server on loopback as a fake broker and point broker.Config.BaseURL at it (plain http is allowed only for loopback). They also set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with t.Setenv to check that the client ignores them.
  • Scripted model. The agent tests use a scriptedModel that implements agent.Model and returns prepared replies in order, with helpers to build text and tool-use messages. A fakeApprover records proposals and returns canned decisions. Together they cover declines, edited proposals, aborts, truncation and MaxTurns without calling any model.
  • Temp directories instead of the real home. config and store tests write under t.TempDir() and set XDG_CONFIG_HOME or XDG_STATE_HOME with t.Setenv. The sshconfig functions take a sshconfig.Paths{SSHDir: ...} value, so tests point SSHDir at a temporary directory and never touch ~/.ssh. Skill override tests build override directories (including escaping symlinks) in a temp directory.
  • Two-handle store tests. Because several Labmill processes share one database, the store tests open the same file twice with store.Open and use both handles, for example to tail events from one handle while the other writes, and to run concurrent UpdateJob calls from two handles and check that no update is lost.
  • Embedded skills. The skill tests load from an in-memory fs.FS for the loader rules and from skills.FS to check that the vendored skills are valid.

items.title: SSH test server: sshtest
items.text:
internal/sshx/sshtest is an in-process SSH server for tests. It mimics a typical campus login flow: keyboard-interactive password, then a Duo-style menu where 1 sends a push. The Duo modes are: no 2FA, push approved after a delay (or a passcode), push never approved, auto-push without a menu (approved or never), not enrolled, and push denied. It also provides:

  • scripted exec commands (Handler functions standing in for sinfo, sbatch, squeue, ...), which receive the arguments verbatim and return an exit status;
  • the sftp subsystem (github.com/pkg/sftp), backed by a real directory;
  • direct-tcpip forwarding, for ProxyJump tests;
  • a known-hosts line, so tests verify host keys without touching the developer's ~/.ssh.

Tests point sshconfig.Paths at a temporary SSHDir, so they stay offline and never use real keys. The helper, the Slurm runner, ssh-exec and the transfers are all tested against this server.

items.title: The end-to-end harness (internal/e2e)
items.text:
internal/e2e holds test code only. A scripted model drives the real agent loop through the real app tools, the Slurm backend over the SSH helper, rclone uploads and downloads through ssh-exec, and the SQLite store, against the in-process SSH server acting as the cluster. The Slurm test walks the full flow: find, stage, upload (approval), draft, submit (approval), status, fetch (approval). It checks the uploaded bytes on the fake cluster, that the approved script is what reached sbatch, the fetched results and the final job state.

Because rclone runs labmill ssh-exec as a child process, the e2e TestMain re-executes the test binary as ssh-exec when LABMILL_E2E_SSHEXEC=1 is set. The tests skip under -short, since they spawn processes.

items.title: Why some tests are excluded from -race
items.text: The e2e tests carry //go:build !race. rclone v1.75.1's external-ssh connection pooling has an internal data race (sshSessionExternal.exited in backend/sftp/ssh_external.go reads cmd.ProcessState while exec.Cmd.Wait writes it), which fires during real transfers. It is not in Labmill's code, so the tests are skipped under the race detector instead of failing it. Run them with plain go test ./internal/e2e/. The transfer tests work around the same race. Everything else is race-tested: go test -race ./... still covers the store, the helper, the agent and the TUI.

items.title: Live smoke test
items.text:
internal/backend/slurm/live_test.go (TestLiveReadOnly) parses real sinfo and squeue output from a real Slurm cluster. It is skipped unless LABMILL_LIVE=1. It needs an already-authenticated OpenSSH ControlMaster that you opened yourself (set LABMILL_LIVE_ALIAS to its SSH alias; there is no default and the test skips when it is unset; check with ssh -O check <alias>), and it only runs read-only commands.

LABMILL_LIVE=1 LABMILL_LIVE_ALIAS=<alias> go test -run TestLiveReadOnly ./internal/backend/slurm/

The Slurm live tests that submit (LABMILL_LIVE_SUBMIT=1) send only short CPU jobs named labmill-live-* and cancel only their own jobs. internal/launch/live_guard_test.go holds the guard approver used by the live runs; it approves only steps that stay inside the test's own folder.

items.title: Live S3 check
items.text:
TestLiveS3 (internal/transfer/live_s3_test.go) runs Labmill's real UploadS3/DownloadS3 against real S3. It never creates or deletes buckets or objects (re-runs overwrite). Create the buckets yourself first (private, public access blocked; one with default SSE-KMS using the aws/s3 key), then:

LABMILL_LIVE=1 LABMILL_LIVE_S3=1 LABMILL_LIVE_S3_BUCKET=<plain bucket> \
  LABMILL_LIVE_S3_KMS_BUCKET=<kms bucket> [LABMILL_LIVE_S3_REGION=us-west-2] [LABMILL_LIVE_S3_PROFILE=<profile>] \
  go test -run TestLiveS3 -v ./internal/transfer/

Subtests: plain (small files, an empty file, a 210 MiB random file uploaded multipart in 42 parts, download, byte compare, re-upload skips); kms-default-encryption (the same on a bucket whose default encryption is SSE-KMS); kms-explicit-sse (SSE: "aws:kms"); wrong-region (region set to us-east-1 for a us-west-2 bucket).

Findings from the first runs:

  • Bug found and fixed: on a bucket with default SSE-KMS the ETag is a 32-hex non-MD5, and rclone (not told about the encryption) failed the upload with md5 hashes differ; multipart would fail the same way. UploadS3/DownloadS3 now detect that error and repeat once with rclone's checksum comparison and multipart-ETag check off (S3's Content-MD5 check on every request and part, and Labmill's size check, stay). DownloadS3 repeats only after a HeadObject shows the failing object is KMS (or SSE-C) encrypted, and then sets server_side_encryption on the source so rclone checks the md5chksum metadata where present; it never ignores checksums, and a mismatch on any other object is an error. Covered offline by TestS3NonMD5ETag, TestS3NonMD5ETagCorruptBodyFails (a body damaged after Content-MD5 was set is still rejected) and TestS3DownloadMismatchWithoutKMSFails (fake S3 with bogus ETags).
  • rclone may remove its own failed upload under the prefix; the test never deletes anything itself.
  • Wrong region: rclone follows S3's redirect, no error, so there is nothing to explain.
  • A named non-default profile (LABMILL_LIVE_S3_PROFILE) works. SSO profiles: not tested (no SSO profile in ~/.aws/config).

items.title: Fuzzing
items.text:
FuzzQuoteSplit in internal/backend/review_m7_test.go checks that backend.Quote and backend.SplitWords round-trip for arbitrary strings. As an ordinary test it runs the seed corpus on every go test. To fuzz for real:

go test ./internal/backend -run '^$' -fuzz FuzzQuoteSplit -fuzztime 30s

items.title: Other conventions
items.text:
• TUI tests use Bubble Tea's teatest helpers and an injectable clock (model.now), so the half-second key grace after a modal opens can be tested without sleeping.
  • Cross-platform code. Privacy rules, the helper's lock and spawn code sit behind build tags. make check only cross-compiles them for Windows and macOS; some checks need real hardware.

items.title: Build targets and test setup
items.text:
Minimum Go 1.26 (go.mod: go 1.26.0, toolchain go1.26.8), which Charm v2 needs. The Makefile exports GOTOOLCHAIN=auto.

make check                     # the gate: gofmt check, go vet, go test ./..., cross build+vet for windows/amd64 and darwin/arm64
make build                     # bin/labmill (TUI)
go test ./internal/skill -run TestLoad      # one package / one test
go test -race ./...            # needed when touching goroutines, the store or the helper
go test ./internal/e2e/        # e2e tests are //go:build !race (rclone's own data race) and skip under -short
make docs                      # zensical build --strict (zensical.toml, docs/ -> site/; uv tool install zensical)
make gui-linux                 # bin/labmill-gui, tags desktop,production,webkit2_41 (cgo + webkit2gtk-4.1); not in make check
make gui-smoke / gui-selftest  # run the GUI under a throwaway HOME in tmp/, on a hidden Xvfb display (LABMILL_GUI_VISIBLE=1 shows it); selftest asserts on the real DOM
make gui-windows / gui-windows-selftest   # cross-built exe, self-test on the Windows host via WSL interop (WebView2)
  • Live tests are opt-in (skip otherwise): LABMILL_LIVE=1 (read-only, needs a live ControlMaster for LABMILL_LIVE_ALIAS), LABMILL_LIVE_SUBMIT=1 for job-submitting tests.
  • Offline test doubles: internal/sshx/sshtest (in-process SSH server that mimics a password + Duo-menu login, with scripted exec commands, sftp and direct-tcpip), agent/agenttest (fake broker), review_test.go regressions; tests needing rclone's ssh-exec child re-exec the test binary (LABMILL_E2E_SSHEXEC / LABMILL_TEST_SSHEXEC).
  • GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/): see CI.

items.title: GUI self-tests
items.text:
make gui-selftest runs the Wails GUI on a hidden Xvfb display. make gui-windows-selftest runs the cross-built exe in WebView2 on the Windows host through WSL interop; its window is never shown (no focus change, no taskbar button; the tray icon shows briefly) and the test proves that with IsWindowVisible/GetForegroundWindow on the app's own windows. The self-test also covers the jobs panel divider (section 6b: keys, drag, double-click reset, the saved width through SettingsAPI); the prefs field has Go tests in internal/gui/prefs_test.go (round trip, clamping). Details in gui.md.

Startup timing (internal/startup): every startup step records a mark or span; the lines (startup: <step> <ms> ms) go to labmill.log when the chat is usable (again after 20 s for the background steps) and are printed by the self-test. LABMILL_GUI_TIMING=1 make gui-selftest (or gui-windows-selftest) also runs the real launch.Build on a persistent home per site next to the executable, labmill-selftest-timing-home-<domain>, reused across runs so the second run is a warm start (LABMILL_GUI_TIMING_SITE=<domain> picks the site profile, default generic), so the numbers cover the whole startup.

items.title: TUI stack: Charm
items.text:
CLAUDE.md keeps the rule: Charm v2 libraries, charm.land/... import paths, never the v1 github.com/charmbracelet/... paths (Harmonica has no v2).

The TUI is built on Charm libraries. Every library except Harmonica is on v2, and the v2 releases use the charm.land/... vanity import paths, not github.com/charmbracelet/.... Don't mix in v1 imports. Many examples online still show the old paths and v1 APIs.

Library Import path GitHub Role in Labmill Bubble Tea charm.land/bubbletea/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea TUI framework (Elm-style model/update/view) for the chat pane and job dashboard Bubbles charm.land/bubbles/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbles Ready-made components: textarea for chat input, viewport, list, table, spinner, progress Huh charm.land/huh/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/huh Forms and prompts: the confirm-before-moving-data step, choosing a cluster, the clusters.yaml setup wizard, and asking for the inputs a skill needs Lip Gloss charm.land/lipgloss/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss Styling and layout (panes, borders, colors) Glamour charm.land/glamour/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/glamour Renders markdown in the terminal: Claude's replies, skill reference docs, and generated scripts shown for review Log charm.land/log/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/log Logging, especially for headless Agent mode Harmonica github.com/charmbracelet/harmonica (v0.2, no v2) https://github.com/charmbracelet/harmonica Spring-physics animation for progress and transitions Wish charm.land/wish/v2 https://github.com/charmbracelet/wish Serves Bubble Tea apps over SSH. Using it would add a server component, which conflicts with the "nothing left running permanently" rule in CLAUDE.md ("Design constraints to preserve"). Get it decided before relying on it.

The current Charm v2 go.mod files declare go 1.25–1.26, which is why the project minimum is Go 1.26.

items.title: Voice: "Hey Labmill"
items.text:
Status: planned, no code yet. It needs real macOS and Windows hardware. It is GUI-only (Windows and macOS); the TUI is not part of it. CLAUDE.md keeps a short summary.

Saying "Hey Labmill" brings the Wails GUI chat box to the front, puts the cursor in it, and presses the OS dictation keystroke so the user can speak the request. The TUI is not part of this. The sequence is the same on both platforms:

  1. A local wake word fires.
  2. The listener pauses so it doesn't re-trigger or fight dictation for the mic.
  3. Labmill shows the window and focuses the chat input. Focus comes first, because dictation types into whatever has focus.
  4. Labmill presses the dictation keystroke.
  5. Dictated text lands in the chat box.
  6. The text is corrected (below), the user confirms, and the listener resumes.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
• Wake word: Windows speech recognition (Windows.Media.SpeechRecognition) with a one-phrase list constraint. It works offline, with no license and nothing to install. Go reaches it through a small WinRT/COM shim. Don't build on the legacy Windows Speech Recognition desktop app, which is deprecated in Windows 11.
  • Keystroke: Win+H, injected with SendInput: VK_LWIN down, H down and up, VK_LWIN up.
  • Focus: Windows restricts SetForegroundWindow for background processes and may only flash the taskbar. Use a known workaround (AttachThreadInput to the foreground thread, or a harmless injected key first) and verify it on Windows 11.
  • Did it open? Check for the voice-typing window with UI Automation, or wait for text in the chat input.

items.title: macOS
items.text:
• Wake word: Apple's Speech framework (SFSpeechRecognizer) with requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true, streaming from AVAudioEngine and matching "hey labmill" in the partial results. Use contextualStrings to bias it toward "labmill". Wails on macOS already needs cgo, so add an Objective-C shim.
  • Permissions: the app needs Microphone and Speech Recognition (TCC usage strings in the .app bundle's Info.plist) plus Accessibility, which posting keystrokes requires (CGPreflightPostEventAccess / CGRequestPostEventAccess). This is one more reason voice is GUI-only: a bare TUI binary can't get these prompts cleanly.
  • Keystroke: press the user's configured dictation shortcut (System Settings → Keyboard → Dictation → Shortcut). Read it from user defaults; which defaults domain and key hold it still needs checking. Then post it with CGEventPost:
  • Press Control twice: two kCGEventFlagsChanged down/up pairs for kVK_Control (0x3B), within about 300 ms.
  • Press Right Command twice: the same with kVK_RightCommand (0x36). For Left or Either Command, use kVK_Command (0x37).
  • Press Fn/🌐 twice or Microphone key: these usually can't be synthesized, because Fn and the mic key are handled below the CGEvent layer. Either suggest the user switch the shortcut to Control or Right Command twice (ask; never change system settings silently), or use the fallback.
  • Fallback when no keystroke works: send startDictation: to the first responder inside Labmill's own process ([NSApp sendAction:@selector(startDictation:) to:nil from:nil], the action behind Edit → Start Dictation…). It needs no Accessibility permission, but the Wails app must keep the standard Edit menu.
  • Did it open? If Dictation is turned off in System Settings, say so and offer to open that settings pane. Otherwise wait for text in the chat input.

items.title: Self-correction (both platforms)
items.text:
• Misheard words. Dictation mangles domain terms ("S batch", "lab mill", folder names). Messages from voice are tagged, and Claude corrects them using a vocabulary of cluster names from clusters.yaml, local folder names and Slurm terms. The corrected text appears in the chat box for the user to confirm or edit before anything runs.
  • Dictation failures. Dictation may not open, the mic may be muted or busy, or no text may arrive within a few seconds. Retry once, using the fallback path on macOS, and if that fails, tell the user exactly what went wrong.
  • Ambiguity. If the corrected request is still unclear, ask a clarifying question instead of guessing.

Privacy: wake-word detection stays on the device. Windows voice typing may use Microsoft's online speech service. macOS Dictation runs on-device on Apple silicon for supported languages and otherwise may go to Apple. The resulting text goes to Claude like any typed message.

items.title: User guide
items.text:
Labmill lets you describe a compute job in plain language and then does the rest: it finds your data, sends it to a cluster, starts the job, watches it, and brings the results back. You don't write job scripts and you don't need to know the terminal.

Where Labmill stands today

The text-based chat window (the "TUI") works on macOS and Linux. The desktop app (GUI) is built and being tested on Windows and Linux; this guide describes the text window, and the desktop app has the same approvals. The "Hey Labmill" voice feature and the headless Agent mode are planned, not available yet. See Voice.

items.title: What you need
items.text:
• A computer (a laptop is fine).
  • An account on a Slurm cluster at your institution, with its two-factor sign-in set up if your institution uses one (for example a push to your phone). Labmill doesn't create accounts. It uses the one you already have.
  • Your own Anthropic API key in the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable, or, for invited testers, a connected Labmill account (see Starting Labmill and signing in).
  • Your cluster user name and password.

items.title: What Labmill does without asking, and what it never does without asking
items.text:
Needs your approval every time. Labmill shows you exactly what it wants to do and waits for you to say yes:

Action What you are shown Uploading files The list of files, their sizes, and the destination on the cluster (for example bigcluster:~/labmill/segmentation, where ~ is your home folder there) Submitting a job The full job script, which you can edit before approving Cancelling a job Which job will be cancelled and where Downloading results Which files, from where, to which folder on your computer

The default answer on every approval screen is Decline, so pressing Enter by mistake doesn't send anything.

If you don't want to confirm each step. The checkbox Approve everything automatically (next to Send in the desktop app, or /autoapprove on in the terminal) is off by default. When it is on, Labmill approves every step above for you, a banner stays visible, and each step shows in the chat as "Auto-approved: ...". Reading key or token files, questions from Labmill and logins still ask. See Settings. The checkbox Download results automatically next to it (/autodownload on in the terminal) brings the results of a finished job to your results folder by itself; see Settings.

Done without asking, because it only looks. Labmill can search the folders you chose (or your home folder) for folders that match what you describe. It sees file names, folder sizes and short previews, never whole files:

  • For a document or code file (a README, a script, a build file) it can read a page at a time, up to 200 lines or 16 KiB per page, in files up to 1 MiB. Values that look like passwords, tokens or API keys are replaced by a placeholder before anything is shown.
  • For a data file (a CSV, a table) it reads only a short sample from the start, so it can see the column names.

It can also check the cluster's queues, your job status and your job logs. Ask it things like "What's in my queue on bigcluster?" or "What did I run last week?" and it lists your jobs there, including ones you started yourself outside Labmill.

Commands on the cluster. To answer questions and diagnose problems, Labmill can run commands on the cluster's login computer on your behalf.

  • Commands that only look run at once, on any file or folder your account is allowed to read. These are things like listing queues, listing or reading a file, checking disk space, listing software modules, or reading a job log.
  • Commands that could change something show you the exact line that will run and wait for your approval.
  • Reading a file that holds keys or tokens (for example an SSH private key or a cloud credential) asks you first, because what it prints would be sent to Claude. The approval box says so.
  • Labmill doesn't add its own limits on what you may run on the cluster. What your account may do there is decided by your institution's administrators, as always.

Never touched on your own computer. Labmill ignores hidden folders (names starting with a dot, such as .ssh), key and password files (for example id_*, *.pem, *.key, .env, .netrc, or names containing "secret" or "credential"), and on macOS and Windows the system folders (Library, AppData). These are never listed, previewed, uploaded or written to.

Your password and two-factor code are typed into Labmill's sign-in box, used for that sign-in only, and never saved to disk.

items.title: Connect the client to your Labmill account
items.text: You can connect Labmill to your account at app.labmill.org. Then your finished jobs show in the web app: their state, times and resources, and the cause category of a failed job. This is optional. Labmill works the same without it, and while it is not connected it sends nothing to Labmill.
path: Connect the client to your Labmill account

items.title: What is sent, and what is not
items.text:
When a job ends (completed, failed, timed out, out of memory or cancelled), Labmill sends one record of it to your account:

  • the cluster (as the HPC system that the web app knows);
  • the Slurm state and, for a time-out or out-of-memory failure, that category;
  • when the job was submitted, started and ended, and how long it waited in the queue;
  • the resources the job asked for: CPUs, memory, GPUs and GPU type, time limit, nodes;
  • the partition;
  • the names and versions of the software modules it loaded (for example samtools/1.21).

Labmill does not send:

  • job scripts or commands;
  • data files, program code or file names;
  • job names, folder names or paths;
  • environment variables, passwords, keys or tokens;
  • log lines or the failure causes it remembers on your computer.

Only jobs that end after you connect are sent. Jobs from before stay on your computer only.
path: Connect the client to your Labmill account

items.title: Connect
items.text:
1. Sign in at app.labmill.org and open Settings > Program tokens.
  2. Make a token. The web app shows it once. It starts with lmt_ and is valid for one year.
  3. Give it to Labmill:
    • Desktop app: open Settings > Labmill account, paste the token into Program token and click Connect.
    • Terminal: run labmill login and paste the token when Labmill asks. The token is not shown while you paste it.

Labmill checks the token with your account before it keeps it. A wrong or revoked token is refused with a message.

The token is kept on this computer only, in account.json next to clusters.yaml (~/.config/labmill/account.json). Only your user account can read the file. Labmill sends the token only to app.labmill.org, over an encrypted connection.
path: Connect the client to your Labmill account

items.title: Check the connection
items.text:
• Desktop app: Settings > Labmill account > Check connection.
  • Terminal: labmill whoami shows the account, since when it is connected, and how many job records were sent or are waiting.
path: Connect the client to your Labmill account

items.title: When the computer is offline
items.text:
Labmill keeps the records in its job database on your computer and sends them when it can reach your account again. It tries again after 1 minute, then after longer pauses, up to 6 hours. The same job is never stored twice in your account, also when two Labmill windows are open.

If your account does not know a cluster yet, its records wait and Labmill tries again later. If the account refuses the token (for example, you revoked it), the records wait until you connect with a new token.
path: Connect the client to your Labmill account

items.title: Disconnect
items.text:
• Desktop app: Settings > Labmill account > Disconnect.
  • Terminal: labmill logout.

Labmill deletes the token from this computer and sends nothing after that. Records that were not sent stay on your computer. To stop the token from working anywhere, revoke it at Settings > Program tokens in the web app.
path: Connect the client to your Labmill account

items.title: Using the same know-how in Claude Code
items.text: Labmill's knowledge about clusters is not locked inside the app. It is written as skills, plain text folders that Claude Code can read too. If you already use Claude Code in a terminal, or prefer it to a chat window, you can install the skills and ask Claude to do the same kind of work. In that case Claude runs the cluster commands for you in your own terminal, and Labmill is not involved.
path: Using the same know-how in Claude Code

items.title: The skills
items.text:
There are three folders to install:

Skill What it knows slurm-user Slurm: writing and submitting batch scripts, choosing partitions, reading job status and failures. research-computing Everything that isn't specific to one scheduler: environments, containers, file systems and storage, moving data, getting help and writing a good support ticket. your institution's site skill (for example site-example-edu) The facts that differ from place to place: login addresses, sign-in and two-factor steps, cluster names, storage folders, how to get an account.

The first two are the same for everyone and contain no institution-specific facts. The site skill carries those. If your institution has no site skill, use the generic one (site-generic); it tells Claude to ask you for the missing facts and to look them up on the cluster.
path: Using the same know-how in Claude Code

items.title: Where they come from
items.text: The generic skills are in the skills/ folder of the Labmill client project, and the generic site skill is in sites/generic/. The Labmill app includes the same files, so the app and Claude Code give the same advice. Site skills for a particular institution are not part of the Labmill client. Ask whoever set up Labmill for your institution for your site skill, or use the generic one.
path: Using the same know-how in Claude Code

items.title: Installing them
items.text:
Claude Code looks for skills in a .claude/skills/ folder, either in a project or in your home folder (~/.claude/skills/ on macOS and Linux, %USERPROFILE%\.claude\skills\ on Windows). Copy the three folders there, one folder per skill, and keep the folder names. Copy the whole site folder: it points to files inside its cluster folders.

Then start a new Claude Code session and ask in plain words, for example "why is my job pending?" or "run my training script on a GPU". Claude loads the right skill when it needs it.
path: Using the same know-how in Claude Code

items.title: What differs from the Labmill app
items.text:
• The app has built-in approval boxes for uploads, job submissions and downloads. In Claude Code, Claude asks for permission to run each command the way Claude Code always does, so read what it wants to run before you allow it.
  • The app keeps your cluster login open for you. In Claude Code you sign in (with your two-factor step) in your terminal first, as you would for any cluster work. See using the cluster from a terminal.
  • The skills hold the same checks and lessons as the app: how to choose a partition and the software, how to check that a download arrived intact, how to diagnose a failed job.
path: Using the same know-how in Claude Code

items.title: Keeping them current
items.text: The skill files in your .claude/skills/ folder are yours; nothing updates them behind your back. To get newer ones, copy the folders again from the Labmill project. The Labmill app can update its own copy automatically, see Know-how updates.
path: Using the same know-how in Claude Code

items.title: Clusters and sign-in
items.text: Labmill uses your own cluster account. It has no accounts of its own. It supports Slurm clusters only.

items.title: What Labmill needs from you
items.text:
• Your home institution (a list in the first-run form, or enter the login host yourself).
  • Your user name on the cluster.
  • Your password and your two-factor step, when the cluster asks for them.

The first-run form is in Starting Labmill and signing in.

items.title: SSH
items.text:
Labmill signs in over SSH. It does its own SSH. It does not start the ssh program.

  • Labmill writes its connection settings in OpenSSH format to ~/.ssh/config.d/labmill.
  • It adds one Include line at the top of ~/.ssh/config. It makes a backup of your file first.
  • It never changes entries that you wrote yourself.
  • Because the format is standard, ssh <alias> works in a terminal too. See Using the saved SSH settings in a terminal.
  • Labmill keeps one login open while you work. A small helper program holds it and exits about 10 minutes after you stop.
  • Host keys go to your normal ~/.ssh/known_hosts file. The first time, Labmill asks "Do you trust this server?". The default answer is No.

items.title: Two-factor sign-in
items.text:
1. Labmill asks for your password in its own box. The characters are hidden.
  2. If your institution uses a push to your phone, Labmill picks that option. Approve the push on your phone. Labmill waits up to about a minute.
  3. Labmill keeps the login open. It does not ask again for each upload or job.

Passwords, two-factor codes and key passphrases are never written to disk.

If your password is wrong, Labmill tries once and stops, so that your account is not locked. If no push arrives, see Troubleshooting.

items.title: Clusters that accept only SSH keys
items.text: Labmill guides you through a one-time key setup. It looks for keys you already have, can create a new key, and shows you the public key to register. Labmill never overwrites an existing key. The full steps are in Starting Labmill and signing in.

items.title: Add or change a cluster
items.text:
• In the desktop app: Settings > Clusters. See Settings.
  • In the terminal app: type /settings to see the settings. Ask Labmill in the chat to set up another cluster. It shows the details for your approval.
  • By hand: edit ~/.config/labmill/clusters.yaml. Labmill reads it when it starts.

Before the first change, Labmill saves a copy of clusters.yaml next to it.

items.title: Open a terminal on the cluster
items.text: labmill shell <cluster> opens a terminal on the login node while Labmill is signed in. The desktop app has a Terminal button. What you type there is not sent to the assistant.

items.title: Contact
items.text:
Write to help@labmill.org.

Please tell us:

  • your computer (macOS, Windows or Linux) and the Labmill version (labmill version);
  • what you asked Labmill to do, and what happened;
  • the report from Copy diagnostics (desktop app, Settings > About and diagnostics). It holds no passwords, keys, sign-in codes or user names.

Do not send passwords, API keys or private keys by email.

The privacy policy is at https://labmill.org/privacy/. Releases and downloads are at https://github.com/labmill/labmill-client/releases.

To contribute code, read CONTRIBUTING.md. We test pull requests by hand.

items.title: Data transfer and checks
items.text: Labmill never sends a file until you approve the list and the destination.

items.title: Before the upload
items.text:
1. Labmill looks in the folders you chose (or your home folder) and shows what it found: folder, number of files, size, example file names.
  2. It makes a manifest: the paths, sizes and checksums of the files.
  3. You see an approval box with the file list, the totals and the destination, for example bigcluster:~/labmill/segmentation. The default answer is Decline.

Hidden folders, system folders and files that look like keys or passwords are not chosen. See Privacy.

items.title: How files move
items.text:
• Labmill sends files one by one with a built-in copy of rclone. It does not start a separate rclone program.
  • It never syncs and never deletes files.
  • The default way is SFTP, through the cluster's transfer host (files_host) when you have one.
  • S3 is optional. See Starting Labmill and signing in.
  • A progress line shows the amount, the speed and the time left.

items.title: Long transfers
items.text:
• Your computer does not go to sleep while a transfer runs.
  • If a transfer breaks, Labmill starts it again by itself, up to three times. It skips files that are already there.
  • If it still fails, the chat tells you.

items.title: Checks on results
items.text:
When you download results:

  1. You approve which files come down and where. The default folder is ~/labmill-results/<job name>.
  2. Labmill compares the SHA-256 checksum of each file with the checksum computed on the cluster.
  3. A file that does not match is kept with the name ending .mismatch. Labmill tells you which file. Nothing is overwritten or deleted. The job is not marked as fetched, so you can fetch it again.
  4. If the cluster cannot compute checksums, Labmill compares file sizes and says so.

You can turn on Download results automatically (off by default). See Settings.

items.title: Limits
items.text: [CHECK: the largest upload Labmill accepts is not a fixed number in the user docs. Ask the dev team if a limit should be written here.]

items.title: The desktop app and the tray
items.text: The Labmill desktop app has the chat on the left and your jobs on the right. You add your data folder, and your code folder if you have one, with the + button in the chat box.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: The hourglass: Labmill is working
items.text:
Labmill always shows when it is busy, so you never have to guess whether it heard you.

While it starts. The window opens with an hourglass and Starting labmill…. The text below it says what Labmill is doing:

Text What Labmill is doing Loading your settings… Reading your cluster settings (the first time, it then asks for your institution and username). Opening the job database… Opening its list of your jobs on this computer. Loading skills… Loading what it knows about your clusters.

If starting takes longer than about 10 seconds, a second line says which step it is still waiting for, for example "Still waiting for: loading skills (14 s)". The chat replaces the hourglass as soon as the window is up; the line under it shows the step still running, and a message you type meanwhile is sent when Labmill has finished starting. On Windows a small Starting labmill… window with a moving bar appears at once, even before the main window, and closes when the main window is ready; the tray icon appears early too; until Labmill is ready its tooltip reads "Labmill is starting…".

After you send a message. A small hourglass with Working… appears under the conversation right away, and changes to the step Labmill is on:

Text What Labmill is doing Connecting to … Logging in to a cluster (a login window or two-factor approval may follow). Waiting for Claude… Waiting for the assistant's answer. Running … Running one of its actions, for example cluster_info or upload_data. Uploads and downloads also show their own progress bar.

After 5 seconds the row also shows how many seconds Labmill has been working, so you can tell it hasn't frozen. The row disappears when the answer starts to appear, and Cancel stays available the whole time.

If your computer is set to reduce motion (Windows: Settings → Accessibility → Visual effects → Animation effects off; Mac: System Settings → Accessibility → Display → Reduce motion), the hourglass stands still. Screen readers announce the status text when it changes.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Approve everything automatically
items.text: Next to Send is a checkbox, Approve everything automatically. It is off by default. When you tick it, a banner appears above the chat: "Auto-approve is on, Labmill approves every step for you", with a Turn off button. From then on Labmill does not show approval screens. Each step appears in the chat as "Auto-approved: ...". Reading key or token files, questions from Labmill and logins still ask. The same switch is on the Settings page, which also explains how it differs from "Run commands on the cluster without asking".
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Download results automatically
items.text:
Next to Approve everything automatically is a second checkbox, Download results automatically. It is off by default, and Labmill remembers your choice. When it is on and a job you started finishes (completed, failed or ran out of time, but not when you cancel it), Labmill brings the job's results to your results folder by itself, in the folder named after the job, and checks every file against the cluster. You do not have to ask and you do not get an approval screen, because a download only brings files to your computer; nothing leaves it.

The chat tells you what came down and where, with an Open folder button, and the job shows as downloaded in the job list. It also works while the window is closed and Labmill runs in the tray. Only what the job produced comes down: files you uploaded, hidden or private-looking files (such as .netrc, .env or token files), environments and caches, and symbolic links are left out, and the chat says how many. Results above 2 GB or 2000 files, or more than your disk can hold (Labmill keeps 10 % free), are not downloaded automatically: the chat says why and you can ask Labmill to fetch them. If you are not signed in to the cluster, Labmill tells you once and downloads at its next check after you sign in; it never opens a sign-in window by itself. If the download fails, the chat says so in plain words and you can ask Labmill to fetch the results. A failed job stays marked as failed. A job is downloaded automatically only once, and only if it finishes while the checkbox is on. The same switch is on the Settings page.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Your data and code folders
items.text:
At the upper left of the box where you type is a + button. Click it (or press Enter or Space on it) to open a small menu:

  • Add data folder… comes first. Many people only have data and want it analyzed: you don't need any code. Labmill can write the analysis code for you, and shows it to you before anything runs.
  • Add code folder… is for when you already have scripts or a program.
  • Below a line, up to five folders you used recently, marked Data: or Code:, so you can switch back quickly.
  • Remove data folder and Remove code folder appear once those folders are set.

The two "Add" items open the usual folder window (Explorer on Windows, Finder on a Mac). Use the arrow keys to move in the menu and Esc to close it.

The chosen folders show as small labels just above your text, data first: Data: ~/…/mri-2026 and Code: ~/…/mri/code. Point at one to see the full path; its × removes it.

You can also drag a folder from Explorer or Finder and drop it onto the chat box. Labmill then asks Add as data folder or Add as code folder (press Enter for data, or Esc to cancel). Drops anywhere else are ignored.

Only the folder's location is used; nothing is copied or uploaded when you choose or drop a folder. Labmill remembers your choice and shows it again the next time you start it. The terminal version of Labmill uses the same folders (see your first job).

Your next message tells Labmill about the chosen folders, and Labmill looks there first when it searches for your data, previews a file, makes the file list for an upload or chooses the software for your code. You still approve every upload as usual.

Some folders can't be chosen: a whole drive, a system folder (such as C:\Windows, Program Files or /usr), a folder that contains your home folder, hidden folders, and folders whose names suggest passwords or keys. Labmill says why just above the chat box.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Opening your results
items.text: After Labmill has downloaded the results of a job, an Open folder button appears in the chat, and the job gets an Open folder button in the job list. It opens the results folder in Explorer, Finder or your Linux file manager.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: A terminal on the cluster
items.text:
The Terminal button at the top right opens a terminal on a cluster's login node, inside Labmill, with no new password or approval while Labmill is signed in. Pick the cluster and press New terminal (with only one cluster, the button opens it at once). Each terminal is a tab; open as many as you like and close a tab with its ×, which ends that session. Back to chat only hides the terminals: they keep running until you close their tabs. In Settings > Clusters every cluster also has a Terminal button.

In the jobs panel, Terminal here opens a terminal in the job's folder on the cluster. Open in system terminal starts your computer's own terminal program (Windows Terminal or the command prompt, Terminal.app, or your Linux terminal) on the cluster instead; it needs the Labmill command-line program (labmill) next to the desktop app or on your PATH, and is hidden when Labmill can't find it.

If Labmill isn't signed in to the cluster, the usual sign-in dialog appears, once. While the assistant is busy with a reply, a terminal can't ask you to sign in: it works only if Labmill is already signed in, and otherwise says to try again when the assistant has finished. Only one terminal connects at a time. Copy and paste work as in any terminal (Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V, or Cmd+C and Cmd+V on a Mac).

The terminal is yours: what you type and see there is not sent to the assistant, shown in the chat or saved by Labmill, and the assistant never uses it. Labmill only records in its log that a terminal was opened and closed on the cluster.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Making the jobs panel wider or narrower
items.text: Between the chat and the jobs panel on the right there is a thin divider. Drag it with the mouse to make the panel wider or narrower, or click it and use the Left and Right arrow keys (Home and End jump to the narrowest and widest). Double-click it to go back to the normal width, 40% of the window. Neither side can become too small to read. Labmill remembers the width together with the window position and opens the window the same way next time. In a very narrow window the jobs panel sits below the chat and there is no divider.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Closing the window
items.text:
Labmill remembers the size and position of its window, and whether it was maximized, and opens it the same way next time. If that spot no longer fits your screens (a monitor was unplugged, for example), the window opens centered at its normal size.

The Labmill desktop app works like OneDrive or Teams: closing its window doesn't quit it. Labmill keeps running in the system tray, so your cluster login stays open and you don't have to type your password and approve the two-factor sign-in again when you come back. Jobs keep being watched while the window is hidden.

Click the window's close button (or press Alt+F4 on Windows, Cmd+W on a Mac). The window disappears, and Labmill keeps running:

  • Windows: the Labmill icon is in the notification area at the right end of the taskbar. If you don't see it, click the small arrow (^) there; you can drag the icon onto the taskbar to keep it visible.
  • Linux: the icon is in your panel's tray, if your desktop has one (KDE and most panels do; GNOME needs the AppIndicator extension). Without a tray, closing the window quits Labmill as before, because there would be no way to bring it back.
  • Mac: there is no tray icon. Labmill behaves like any Mac app: it stays in the Dock when you close the window, a click on the Dock icon shows the window again, and Cmd+Q quits it.

On Windows and Linux, the first time you close the window, Labmill tells you once: "Labmill is still running in the tray to keep your cluster login. Right-click the tray icon and choose Quit to exit."
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Bringing the window back
items.text:
• Click the Labmill tray icon (Windows), or right-click it and choose Open labmill.
  • Or simply start Labmill again: instead of opening a second copy, the running Labmill shows its window.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: The tray menu
items.text:
Right-click the tray icon:

Item What it does Open labmill Shows the window. Settings… Shows the window on the Settings page. Status line For example "2 jobs running · logged in to bigcluster". It is for reading only. Start in the tray when I log in When ticked, Labmill starts hidden in the tray each time you log in to your computer. Off by default. Quit labmill Really quits Labmill.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Quitting
items.text: Right-click the tray icon and choose Quit labmill (on a Mac: the Labmill menu → Quit, or Cmd+Q). A reply that is still being written is stopped, and any question Labmill was waiting for is answered with "no". Your cluster login stays open for about 10 more minutes, in case you start Labmill again, and then closes by itself.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Starting with your computer
items.text:
Start in the tray when I log in (tray menu) is off unless you turn it on. When you turn it on, Labmill adds itself to your own startup list, for your account only and without administrator rights:

  • Windows: an entry named "labmill" in Settings → Apps → Startup (it lives under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run).
  • Mac: a login item file in ~/Library/LaunchAgents.
  • Linux: a labmill.desktop file in ~/.config/autostart.

Turning the option off removes the Windows entry and switches the Mac and Linux files off.

With the option on, Labmill starts hidden in the tray when you log in; click the tray icon when you want the window. If the tray isn't available at that moment, Labmill shows its window instead. While the window is hidden, an approval, a login question or a choice from Labmill brings the window to the front, because nobody would see it otherwise; a job notice does not (see the tray's status line).

There is no start-in-tray option on a Mac, because a Mac has no tray icon.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: The to-do list
items.text: For a request with several steps (for example scan your code, choose the software, upload your data, submit, monitor, fetch the results), Labmill shows a short to-do list above the message box and keeps it up to date as it works. ☐ is a step still to do, ◐ is the step in progress (with what Labmill is doing right now), and ☑ is done. You can collapse or expand the list with its title button (keyboard: Tab to it, then Space or Enter). When every step is done, the list stays through your next message and then disappears; it also disappears when a request is canceled or fails. One-step questions don't get a list.
path: The desktop app and the tray

items.title: Failed jobs
items.text: When a job fails, Labmill finds out why.

items.title: Ask
items.text: Type "why did job 12 fail?". You can also use the job list in the desktop app: click Logs or Status.

items.title: What Labmill looks at
items.text:
Labmill collects facts only. It does not change anything on the cluster. The facts are:

  • the state of the job and its history in Labmill;
  • the record of the scheduler: state, exit code, reason, time used against the limit, memory used against the memory you asked for;
  • the end of the job log (the last 60 lines), with secrets hidden;
  • the start of the job script.

Then the assistant names the likely cause in plain words. It uses the failure patterns in Labmill's skills. For example: out of memory, out of time, a missing module, a file that was not found.

items.title: Fix and resubmit
items.text: Labmill offers to fix the problem and submit the job again. You see the new script and approve it, as for any job.

items.title: Memory on your computer
items.text: Labmill remembers the cause in its job database on your computer only. The next time you draft a job from the same folder on the same cluster, it tells you that an earlier run failed and why. The cause is not sent anywhere except in the chat.

items.title: Preempted jobs
items.text: If a job runs on a preemptible partition, Labmill can submit it again after a preemption, at most twice, then once on a regular partition. You see this plan before you approve the job.

items.title: When the job never starts
items.text: Before you submit, the job review says whether Slurm accepts the script and when it expects the job to start. If Slurm refuses the script, the box shows Slurm's error. You can fix the script first.

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Which clusters does Labmill work with? Slurm clusters only.

Do I need an account with Labmill? No. You use your own cluster account and your own Anthropic API key. A Labmill account at app.labmill.org is optional.

Do I need my own Anthropic API key? Not if you are an invited tester. Without a key, a client connected to your Labmill account (labmill login) uses the Labmill test relay: app.labmill.org sends your requests to Claude with Labmill's key, within a daily limit, and does not store them. This is for testing only. Your own key stays the private choice: Labmill then talks to Anthropic directly and nothing goes through Labmill. When both are there, Labmill uses your own key. See Starting Labmill and signing in.

Is the client linked to my Labmill account? Only if you connect it. Make a program token at app.labmill.org and run labmill login, or paste it in Settings > Labmill account. Then Labmill sends a record of each job that ends: state, times, resources, partition and software modules. It never sends job scripts, data files, program code, names or log lines. See Connect the client to your Labmill account.

Does Labmill cost money? The client is free. It will be open source under the MIT license when it is published. Anthropic bills the API use on your own key (the test relay costs testers nothing). A Labmill account on labmill.org is optional: it costs 6 USD a month, or 35 USD a month for a fully private account (redacted job facts do not help other researchers), plus tax where it applies. See labmill.org/pricing.

Does it send my data to Claude? No. Claude sees file names, sizes, short previews and small samples. Files go to the cluster only after you approve. See Privacy.

Can I check the job script before it runs? Yes. Every script is shown in full. You can edit it before you approve it.

Can I run a job without writing code? Yes. Add a data folder only. Labmill can write the analysis code, and you see it before anything runs.

Can I close the window while a job runs? Yes. The job runs on the cluster. On Windows and Linux the desktop app keeps running in the tray, so your login stays open. See The desktop app and the tray.

Is anything left running on my computer? Only the desktop app in the tray (you quit it from the tray menu) and a small SSH helper that exits about 10 minutes after you stop.

Where are my results? In ~/labmill-results/<job name>.

Is a file I downloaded damaged? Labmill checks each file with a SHA-256 checksum. A file that does not match gets the name ending .mismatch. See Data transfer and checks.

What are the "approve" switches? Run commands on the cluster without asking and Approve everything automatically. Both are off by default. See Settings.

Does it work with Claude Code? The skills are in Claude Code format, so you can use them there too. See Claude Code.

Is voice input available? No. It is planned. See Voice.

How do I update? Download the newest files from the releases page. See Install.

items.title: Your first job
items.text: A typical conversation looks like this. Type in plain words. You can ask follow-up questions at any time.

items.title: Tell Labmill where your data (and code) are (optional)
items.text:
You can point Labmill at the folder with your data, and the folder with your code if you have any, before you start, so you don't have to describe where they are. You don't need code: if you only add a data folder, Labmill offers to write the analysis code for you, and you see that code before anything runs.

  • Desktop app: click the + at the upper left of the chat box and choose Add data folder… (or Add code folder…), or drop a folder from Explorer or Finder onto the chat box and pick "Add as data folder" or "Add as code folder" (see the desktop app).
  • Terminal: type /data ~/data/mri-2026 and, if you have code, /code ~/projects/mri. Tab completes folder names. /data alone shows the current choice, and /data - clears it (the same for /code). The status bar shows Data: … and Code: ….

Choosing a folder sends nothing. Your next message tells Labmill about it, and Labmill then searches there first, can preview a file by its name in the folder, makes upload lists from the data folder, and looks at the code folder to choose the software. Hidden folders, system folders and folders that look like they hold passwords or keys can't be chosen. Labmill remembers the folders between runs. The desktop app and the terminal share them; a change made in one shows in the other the next time it starts.

items.title: 1. Describe the job
items.text:
Train the segmentation model in my Experiments folder on the scans in ~/data/mri-2026, 1 GPU, overnight.

Labmill may ask a few questions if something is unclear, such as which script to run or how long it should run. Not every job needs your data: you can also ask for something like a quick GPU check, and Labmill skips the upload steps.

As soon as you send a message, Labmill shows that it's working and what it's waiting for, such as "Connecting to bigcluster…" or "Waiting for Claude…". The desktop app shows a small hourglass under the conversation (see the hourglass); the terminal shows a spinner with the same text in the status bar. After 5 seconds both also show how long it has been working.

items.title: 2. Labmill finds your data
items.text:
Labmill looks through your chosen data and code folders (or, if you chose none, your home folder) for folders that match your description and shows what it found: the folder, how many files, how big it is, and a few example file names. It sees names and sizes, and it can preview a file if that helps: a short sample from the start of a data file, or a page at a time of a document or script (see the overview). Hidden folders and key files are skipped (see the overview).

You confirm the right folder, or tell Labmill which one you meant. Nothing has left your computer yet. Labmill only makes a list of the files, with their sizes and checksums, so it can later verify that everything arrived intact.

items.title: 3. Labmill picks where to run
items.text: Labmill looks at what each cluster offers (partitions, GPU types, how busy it is) and suggests one. You can say "use the other cluster" or name a partition.

items.title: 4. Approve the upload
items.text:
A box covers the screen with the title of what Labmill wants to do, for example "Upload 14,212 files (86 GB) from /home/you/data/mri-2026 to bigcluster:~/labmill/segmentation". A destination written cluster:~/folder is inside your home folder on the cluster. You can also ask for an absolute group folder such as /data/mygroup/data; hidden folders (starting with a dot) and system folders are refused.

  • Below the title is a breakdown by top-level folder, then the file list (the first 200 lines, then "and K more") and the totals. Scroll with PgUp/PgDn or the arrow keys. The hint line at the bottom says when scrolling is possible.
  • Choose with ←/→: Approve or Decline. Decline is selected by default. Press Enter to confirm your choice. Esc declines right away.
  • If you decline, nothing is sent, and Labmill is told you declined. You can also tell Labmill why (it asks in one line; press Enter to send or Esc to skip), and it will adjust its plan.
  • If the window is too small to show the whole approval, Labmill asks you to enlarge it. Only Esc (decline) works until then.

While the data moves, Labmill shows live progress in the style of rclone's stats, for example Transferred: 1.2 GiB / 4.0 GiB, 30%, 45 MiB/s, ETA 1m02s · Files: 3 / 10 · now: data/part-003.csv. In the desktop app it is a bar above the input; in the terminal app it takes the status line. When it ends, the result shows a summary such as Transferred 4.0 GiB in 1m31s (45 MiB/s), 10 files, plus a line starting with rclone-lib:. That line holds the transfer's parameters in rclone's own syntax. Labmill has rclone built in as a library and starts no separate rclone process, so rclone-lib: marks it as Labmill's. To repeat the same transfer with a stand-alone rclone, replace rclone-lib: with rclone. The line never contains passwords or keys, and it is not part of what you approve. On Windows, PowerShell 5.1 mangles the quotes in the --sftp-ssh value; use PowerShell 7.3 or newer for that command.

Keys pressed in the first half second after the box opens are ignored, on purpose. See the keyboard reference.

Files go through the cluster's transfer computer (the approval names it), which has its own sign-in like the first one, with its own two-factor approval. After that you aren't asked again while the login stays open. A progress line shows how it is going.

Long transfers. While a transfer runs, your computer does not go to sleep. If a transfer breaks (the network drops or the sign-in is lost), Labmill starts it again by itself, up to three times. It skips the files that are already there. If it still fails, the chat tells you.

items.title: 5. Labmill drafts the job script
items.text: Labmill writes the job script (what the cluster runs) from your request, with the right number of GPUs, time limit and working folder. It runs in the folder you just uploaded.

items.title: Software for Slurm jobs
items.text: The assistant uses the software that the cluster already offers (its modules) first. If the job needs something else, it can use a Python virtual environment, a conda environment or an Apptainer image. Labmill builds it once, in the software folder of your institution or in .labmill/envs in your home folder. Later jobs use it again. Labmill never removes it. The job script shows the steps, and you approve them like the rest of the script.

items.title: When the job needs a named program
items.text: If your job needs a program or library by name (for example a compiler or a particular analysis tool) and runs on Slurm, Labmill first looks at what the cluster already provides. It searches the cluster's software list (the "modules"), then any other software your institution installs centrally, and only after that considers setting up your own environment or using a container. Most of these searches only look and run without asking; a check that needs a full login on the cluster is shown to you first. If a ready-made version exists, the job script uses that exact version, so the same job runs the same way next time.

items.title: When the code has no run script
items.text: Sample code often comes with a README and a build file (CMakeLists.txt, Makefile, setup.py, requirements.txt) but no script that builds and runs it. Labmill does not guess script names and does not ask you how to run it. It lists the folder, reads the README and the build files page by page, and works out the steps. It uploads your folder as it is, and writes the missing scripts (for example labmill-build.sh and labmill-run.sh) into the job's folder on the cluster, never on your computer. They are shown to you below the job script when you approve the job, and you can edit them there. Labmill creates them just before the job is submitted. If a file with that name already exists on the cluster with other content, Labmill does not overwrite it and uses another name. Folder names with spaces, such as OneDrive - Example University, are fine.

items.title: If a file does not answer
items.text: Files kept in a cloud folder (such as OneDrive, with "files on demand") or on a network drive can stop answering when the drive is offline or the file is only a placeholder. Labmill does not wait for such a file: after a few seconds it skips that file, tells you which one, and carries on with the rest. Make the file available offline (or reconnect the drive) and ask again. If a drive stays stuck, quit Labmill from the tray (or the terminal) and start it again after reconnecting.

items.title: 6. Approve the job
items.text:
Before anything is submitted, Labmill shows the whole script in an approval box. Here you can edit the script directly: the cursor starts inside the text. Press Tab to move to the buttons, ←/→ to choose Approve or Decline, Enter to confirm, and Tab again to return to editing. If you change the text, what you edited is what gets submitted. Decline is again the default.

If the text contains tabs or hidden characters, Labmill warns you that the editor shows them differently, and that an edit submits the text as shown.

items.title: The check before you submit
items.text: The approval box also shows a check that Labmill ran with Slurm. It says that Slurm accepts the script and when it expects the job to start. If Slurm rejects the script, the box shows Slurm's error, so you can fix the script before you submit. If the check cannot run, the box says so. You can still approve.

items.title: 7. Check progress
items.text:
Once the job is submitted, Labmill tells you its number (for example "job #12") and the job runs in the background. The chat is free right away: you can ask questions, start another job, or just wait.

While Labmill is open, it checks your running jobs about every 45 seconds. When one finishes, fails or is cancelled, a short line appears in the chat, for example "Job #12 (train) on bigcluster finished. Ask me to fetch the results." These checks never ask you to sign in. If you are not signed in to the cluster at that moment, Labmill skips the check and tries again later.

Ask "how is my job doing?" or "show me the log of job 12", and Labmill reads the job status and the last lines of the log. If you really want Labmill to sit and wait, say "wait for job 12 to finish". It then checks for up to two minutes at a time, and the chat waits with it. Ask again to keep waiting.

Job end notice. When a job ends, the desktop app shows a notification (Settings: Notify me when a job ends, on by default). If jobs ended while Labmill was closed, Labmill lists them in a While you were away notice when you start it. Slurm can also send you an email when a job ends: turn on Email me when a Slurm job ends (off by default). Labmill then adds the email request to the job script, which you see in the review. The email goes to the default address of your institution.

If a job fails. Ask "why did job 12 fail?". The assistant collects the facts: the state, the exit code, the memory and time the job used against what you asked for, and the end of the log. Then it names the likely cause. Labmill remembers the cause on your computer only. The next time you draft a job from the same folder on the same cluster, Labmill tells you that an earlier run failed and why.

Press Tab to open the jobs panel on the right. It lists your recent jobs and refreshes every few seconds. You can close Labmill and come back later: jobs are remembered on your computer, and the cluster keeps the real status.

To stop a job, say "cancel job 12". You approve that too.

In the desktop app, each job in the job list has small buttons: Status, Logs, Fetch (when a job has finished or failed and has a folder on the cluster) and Cancel (while it is waiting or running). A button simply sends the matching message for you, such as "Cancel job #12", so you get the same answers and the same approval boxes as when you type it.

items.title: Long tasks
items.text: A whole job, from finding the data to fetching the results, takes many steps. After a large number of steps in one go (80), Labmill stops with a note such as "I stopped after 80 steps so you can check in. Say 'continue' and I'll go on." This is not an error: type continue and Labmill picks up where it left off.

items.title: While Labmill is answering
items.text: You don't have to wait for an answer to finish before typing the next message. Type it and press Enter (in the desktop app the Send button says Queue while Labmill is busy). The message is held, shown below the chat as "queued", and sent as soon as the current answer ends. Labmill holds one message: if you send another, it replaces the first. Cancelling the current answer doesn't drop the queued message. It is sent right after. In the desktop app, Remove drops it.

items.title: 8. Get your results
items.text:
When the job is finished, say "get the results". Labmill proposes which files to download and where to put them. By default, results go into ~/labmill-results/<job name>. You approve the download, and the files appear in that folder.

After the download, Labmill compares each file's SHA-256 checksum with the one computed on the cluster, so you know nothing was damaged on the way. If a file doesn't match, Labmill keeps your copy under a name ending in .mismatch (nothing is deleted or overwritten), tells you which file, and doesn't mark the job as fetched, so you can fetch it again. If the cluster can't compute checksums, Labmill falls back to comparing file sizes and says so. In the desktop app, click Open folder (in the chat or next to the job in the job list) to open it in Explorer, Finder or your file manager.

items.title: Before you start: your Anthropic API key
items.text:
Labmill's assistant is Claude. Labmill talks to Claude with your own Anthropic API key. Set it in your environment before you start Labmill:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

On Windows, set it as a user environment variable (Settings, search for "environment variables"). Labmill reads the key from the environment only. It never writes the key to disk.

Your own key is optional, and it is the private choice: with it, Labmill talks to Anthropic directly and nothing goes through Labmill. Without a key, a client that is connected to a Labmill account (labmill login, see Connect the client to your Labmill account) uses the Labmill test relay: its requests to Claude go through app.labmill.org, which uses Labmill's own Anthropic key. The relay is for testing only, for invited testers, with a daily limit. The relay does not store your requests. The status line shows which one Labmill uses: assistant: own key or assistant: Labmill test relay. With neither a key nor an account, Labmill starts but tells you that it has no assistant yet.

Planning turns use a larger Claude model and the other turns a faster one. To use one model for all turns, set LABMILL_MODEL (for example LABMILL_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5).

If your institution runs a Labmill relay service (a "broker"), set LABMILL_BROKER_URL to its address and LABMILL_BROKER_TOKEN to the token it gave you. Labmill then sends model calls there instead of to Anthropic.

items.title: Start Labmill
items.text:
Open a terminal window, type labmill and press Enter. (If your IT team installed Labmill for you, they will tell you if it starts differently.)

To leave Labmill, press Ctrl+D. If a job is being submitted at that moment, Labmill waits a few seconds so the job is recorded properly.

items.title: The first-run setup
items.text:
The very first time, Labmill shows a short welcome form:

  1. Your home institution. Pick where your cluster account is from the list. You always choose one. Your data mostly lives on your home institution's systems, so Labmill sends work there first. When your institution has a site profile, Labmill knows its login and file transfer computers and how its two-factor sign-in works, and its assistant knows the local details (cluster names, storage folders, software notes). If your institution isn't in the list, choose My institution isn't listed: Labmill then asks for the cluster login computer (the name you would type after ssh, for example login.example.edu). This tells Labmill which institution is your home.
  2. Your account name. Type the user name you use to sign in to the cluster (your institution's username). Use lowercase letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores.
  3. Save these settings? Choose Yes. Labmill saves the cluster addresses and your user name in the standard SSH settings format, in a separate file (~/.ssh/config.d/labmill), and adds one line at the top of your ~/.ssh/config so that file is used. Before changing your own file it makes a backup copy next to it. If you already had a name for the same cluster, Labmill reuses your name and doesn't write a second one. Labmill saves two computers for each Slurm cluster: the login computer and the file transfer computer. Uploads and downloads go through the transfer computer, which you sign in to the same way. The upload and download approval questions name the computer the files travel through. In clusters.yaml the transfer computer is the files_host line. Keep it: if you remove it, Labmill falls back to the login computer, which may not allow file transfers.

You only do this once. Your cluster list is kept in ~/.config/labmill/clusters.yaml, and the institution you chose is its site: line (for example site: example.edu). If clusters.yaml has no site: line (for example settings saved by an older Labmill) or names an institution this Labmill doesn't know, Labmill shows the institution form again with a short explanation and adds only the site: line; your clusters stay as they are. To switch institution later, change the site: line (and the cluster entries), or move clusters.yaml aside and start Labmill again to get the welcome form.

Labmill reads job times in UTC, so you normally don't need to set anything. Only if a Slurm cluster's job start and end times still look wrong (its Slurm ignores the time zone request), add a timezone: line to its entry, for example timezone: Europe/Berlin.

items.title: Coming from yeetl?
items.text: If Labmill has no ~/.config/labmill/clusters.yaml yet, it looks for a yeetl setup on its first start. It copies ~/.config/yeetl/clusters.yaml (only if the file parses) and ~/.ssh/config.d/yeetl. It copies the files and does not move them, so yeetl keeps working. The variables YEETL_MODEL, YEETL_BROKER_URL and YEETL_BROKER_TOKEN are read when the matching LABMILL_ variable is empty.

items.title: The first login
items.text:
Labmill signs in to the cluster the first time it needs it, for example when you ask about queues or when you approve an upload. A small box pops up in the window.

  1. Password. Type your cluster password. The characters are hidden and the password is not saved anywhere.
  2. Two-factor sign-in. If your institution uses a push to your phone, Labmill chooses that option for you. Look at your phone and approve the push notification. Labmill waits up to about a minute.
  3. That's it. Labmill keeps the login open while you work, so you aren't asked again for every upload or job. A small background helper holds the login and closes it by itself about 10 minutes after you stop using Labmill.

items.title: If no push arrives
items.text: After the wait, Labmill tells you that two-factor sign-in did not complete and shows how to set it up. The usual reasons are that you are not enrolled in two-factor sign-in yet (the message shows your institution's setup page, or ask your help desk), your phone is offline, or the push was denied or expired. Fix that and just ask Labmill to try again.

items.title: If the password is rejected
items.text: Labmill tries your password once and stops. It says that the sign-in was denied, repeats your institution's help when there is any, and reminds you to check your password before trying again: many institutions lock the account after repeated failed sign-ins. Labmill will not start another sign-in by itself in that conversation turn. Check or reset your password, then tell Labmill to try again.

items.title: If your cluster accepts only SSH keys
items.text:
Some clusters don't accept passwords at all, only SSH keys. Labmill knows which ones from your institution's profile, and instead of the password box it guides you through the one-time key setup:

  1. Your existing keys. Labmill first looks for a key it can use: the default key files in your .ssh folder (id_ed25519, id_ecdsa, id_rsa), a key your SSH agent holds, or one named in your SSH settings. If a key is protected by a passphrase, Labmill asks for it (the characters are hidden and the passphrase is not saved anywhere). If the cluster already knows the key, you are signed in and nothing else happens.
  2. Reusing a key you already have. Labmill asks the cluster which of your existing keys it already accepts. It sends only the public keys for this and never signs in again just to ask. It checks the keys on this computer and, if you are already signed in to your home institution's cluster, the keys stored in the .ssh folder there. If an accepted key sits on that cluster and not on this computer, Labmill offers to copy it here. The box shows the key file, where it comes from and where it goes, and warns that this puts a copy of a private key on your computer. The choice is No unless you pick Yes. The copy goes into a new file that only you can read (an existing file is never overwritten), and the key's contents are never shown to the assistant or written to the chat. Labmill also tells you whether the key has a passphrase, which it then asks for at sign-in. If the path to the cluster goes through another host that needs a password, Labmill skips this check and says so.
  3. Creating a key. If no existing key is accepted, or you decline the copy, Labmill asks whether to create a new one. The private key stays on this computer in your .ssh folder and Labmill never overwrites an existing key (a new key gets its own name if id_ed25519 is taken). You may protect it with a passphrase, which Labmill then asks for at each sign-in.
  4. Registering the public key. Labmill shows the public key with a Copy button (Ctrl+Y in the terminal app) and your institution's instructions for where to paste it, usually a page on the cluster's website. Do that, then choose I've added it, try again. The public key is meant to be shared; the private key never leaves your computer.
  5. Signing in. Labmill signs in with the key and remembers it in the SSH settings it keeps for you (the same file the terminal's ssh reads), so ssh and sftp work with it too.

If the cluster does not accept the key yet, Labmill asks you again to finish the upload; some registries take a few minutes. Choose Cancel to stop; nothing is lost, and the key stays in your .ssh folder for the next try. On Windows the new key files get the permissions that your user profile folder gives them, which is what the built-in OpenSSH expects.

If the cluster briefly refuses connections. While Labmill checks which of your existing keys the cluster accepts (step 2), the cluster may shut the door for a short time. Clusters often shut the door for a short time after several sign-in tries in a row. Labmill guards against this by asking about a few keys at a time and pausing between tries. If the cluster still refuses, Labmill says so, waits a minute and checks the remaining keys once more. If it is still refused after that, Labmill stops with a message like "is still refusing connections; wait a few minutes and try again". It does not ask you to create a new key in that case, because the problem is the waiting time, not your keys. Wait a few minutes and start again.

items.title: If your password is rejected
items.text: Labmill tells you to check the user name and password. It tries your password once per login, so repeated mistakes don't lock your account.

items.title: The first connection to a cluster: "Do you trust this server?"
items.text:
The first time Labmill connects to a cluster computer, it shows a question like this: "This is the first time you connect to login.example.edu, so Labmill cannot yet check that it is the real server. Its identity fingerprint is SHA256:... Continue and remember this server?"

This is the same check your terminal's ssh does. Every server has a unique fingerprint. By saying Yes, you tell Labmill "this is the right server, remember it". From then on Labmill checks automatically. If your HPC center publishes the fingerprint, you can compare it. Otherwise it is normally safe to continue the first time, from a trusted network.

The default answer is No. If, later, the server's identity changes, Labmill refuses to connect and tells you not to continue, because it can mean someone is intercepting the connection. Contact your HPC support in that case.

Labmill saves the remembered servers in your normal ~/.ssh/known_hosts file.

items.title: S3
items.text:
A cluster entry can name an S3 bucket instead of sending files over SFTP. This suits large data sets. Set transfer: s3 and add an s3 block:

- name: bigcluster
  type: slurm
  ssh_host: bigcluster-login
  transfer: s3
  s3:
    bucket: my-bucket
    prefix: Labmill        # optional: everything Labmill writes goes below this
    region: us-east-1    # optional: default is the region of your AWS profile
    profile: myprofile   # optional: name of your AWS profile
    # endpoint: https://s3.example.edu   # optional: S3-compatible storage
    # sse: aws:kms                       # optional: for buckets that require KMS encryption

If your bucket requires KMS encryption, add sse: aws:kms; to use a specific key, also add kms_key_id (a key ID, ARN or alias). sse: AES256 asks for S3-managed encryption.
