Your S3 credentials come from your AWS profile (aws configure, or aws sso login for single sign-on). They never go in this file, and Labmill refuses a file that has them. Labmill asks you to approve the file list, the full s3://bucket/prefix/folder destination and the AWS profile before anything is sent. It only writes below that folder, never creates buckets, and checks each uploaded object (size and checksum) against your approved list. Results are downloaded the same way, and never replace files you already have.

Labmill does not set up the bucket or give your jobs access to it. Your job must be able to read the bucket itself, for example with credentials on the cluster (see below). Ask your cluster support if you're not sure.

items.title: Use your AWS profile in Slurm jobs
items.text: You can ask Labmill to copy one AWS profile from your computer to the login node of a Slurm cluster, so your jobs can read and write S3. Labmill stores it as a separate section named [labmill-<name>] in ~/.aws/credentials there and leaves your other sections alone. This always asks first, also when Approve everything automatically is on. If the profile uses single sign-on (SSO), Labmill copies temporary keys that expire. Claude never sees the key values. If you have no AWS profile on your computer, run aws configure first. Your institution can turn this off.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Labmill has two programs. Both do the same work and share the same settings and job list.

Program What it is labmill-gui The desktop app: one chat box and a job list. labmill The terminal app (TUI): a chat pane and a job dashboard.

items.title: Download
items.text:
Go to the Labmill releases page. Open the newest release. Download the files for your computer from the Assets list.

Your computer Desktop app Terminal app macOS (Apple silicon) labmill-gui-darwin-arm64 labmill-darwin-arm64 macOS (Intel) not built labmill-darwin-amd64 Windows (64 bit, Intel or AMD) labmill-gui-windows-amd64.exe labmill-windows-amd64.exe Windows on Arm not built labmill-windows-arm64.exe Linux (64 bit, Intel or AMD) labmill-gui-linux-amd64 labmill-linux-amd64 Linux on Arm labmill-gui-linux-arm64 labmill-linux-arm64

The release also has a file SHA256SUMS. It is the only checksum file: there is no .sha256 file for each download. To check a download, compute its SHA-256 checksum and compare it with the line for your file.

sha256sum labmill-linux-amd64        # Linux
shasum -a 256 labmill-darwin-arm64   # macOS
certutil -hashfile labmill-windows-amd64.exe SHA256   # Windows

Labmill is one file. There is no installer yet. Put the file in a folder you keep, for example ~/bin or C:\Tools.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
You need:

  • an account on a Slurm cluster, with its two-factor sign-in if your institution uses one;
  • your own Anthropic API key in the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable, or, for invited testers, a connected Labmill account (see Starting Labmill and signing in).

items.title: macOS
items.text:
The Labmill programs are not signed by Apple at first. macOS blocks them the first time. This is expected.

  1. Open the Terminal app. Go to the folder with the download.
  2. Make the file runnable and remove the download mark: 
    chmod +x labmill-gui-darwin-arm64
xattr -d com.apple.quarantine labmill-gui-darwin-arm64
  3. Start it: ./labmill-gui-darwin-arm64.

Instead of steps 2 and 3, you can Control-click the file in Finder, choose Open, and confirm.

If macOS still says that it cannot check the program, open System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down, and click Open Anyway next to the message about Labmill. Then start the program again and confirm.

Do the same steps for labmill-darwin-arm64 (or -amd64) if you want the terminal app. Run it as ./labmill-darwin-arm64. Rename it to labmill and put it in a folder on your PATH, and you can start it by typing labmill.

The macOS desktop app is a plain program file, not a .app bundle or a .dmg.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
The Windows programs are not signed at first. Windows SmartScreen may show "Windows protected your PC".

  1. Double-click labmill-gui-windows-amd64.exe.
  2. In the SmartScreen window click More info, then Run anyway.

For the terminal app, open PowerShell in the folder and run .\labmill-windows-amd64.exe. Rename the file to labmill.exe and put it in a folder on your PATH to start it with labmill.

Labmill uses the OpenSSH settings of your user profile (~/.ssh). You do not need to install anything else.

items.title: Linux
items.text:
1. Make the file runnable: chmod +x labmill-gui-linux-amd64 labmill-linux-amd64.
  2. Start it: ./labmill-gui-linux-amd64 or ./labmill-linux-amd64.

The desktop app needs the WebKitGTK 4.1 library. On Debian and Ubuntu the package is libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0. [CHECK: confirm the run-time packages on a clean system.]

For the tray icon, your desktop needs a system tray. KDE and most panels have one. GNOME needs the AppIndicator extension. Without a tray, closing the window quits Labmill. See The desktop app and the tray.

items.title: Check that it works
items.text: Run labmill version. It prints Labmill and the version number.

items.title: Updates
items.text: Labmill does not update itself. To update, download the newest files from the releases page and replace the old ones. Your settings and job list stay.

items.title: Remove Labmill
items.text:
Delete the program file. Labmill keeps these files, and you can keep or delete them:

File What it holds ~/.config/labmill/clusters.yaml your cluster list ~/.config/labmill/gui.json desktop app settings ~/.ssh/config.d/labmill the SSH settings Labmill wrote (and one Include line at the top of ~/.ssh/config) ~/.local/state/labmill/ the job list (labmill.db) and the log (labmill.log) ~/labmill-results/ results you downloaded

If you turned on Start in the tray when I log in, turn it off first (tray menu). See The desktop app and the tray.

[CHECK: the paths of the state and config folders on Windows and macOS. The code uses ~/.config/labmill unless XDG_CONFIG_HOME is set, and ~/.local/state/labmill unless XDG_STATE_HOME is set.]

items.title: In the chat
items.text:
Key What it does Enter Send your message (while Labmill is answering: queue it) Alt+Enter (or Ctrl+J) New line in your message without sending Tab Show or hide the jobs panel PgUp / PgDn Scroll the conversation Ctrl+C Stop the current answer or action. Press it a second time to quit Ctrl+D Quit Labmill

While Labmill is working on an answer, you can keep typing. Enter then queues your message, which is shown above the input and sent when the answer ends. Labmill holds one queued message, and a newer one replaces it. Ctrl+C stops the answer but keeps the queued message, which is then sent.

items.title: In an approval box (upload, job script, cancel, download)
items.text:
Key What it does ←/→ (or Tab) Choose Approve or Decline. Decline is selected at first Enter Confirm the selected button ↑/↓, PgUp/PgDn, Home/End Scroll the details when they don't fit Esc Decline right away Ctrl+C Cancel the whole turn (declines the request) Ctrl+D Quit Labmill

When you edit a job script, the cursor starts in the text. Tab moves to the buttons, and Tab again goes back to the text. Esc still declines.

items.title: In a choice box
items.text:
When Labmill offers you choices (for example "use the cluster's Python module" or "make your own environment"), pick one with the arrow keys and Enter, a number key, or a click. You don't have to type the answer.

Key What it does ↑/↓ (or Tab) Move between the options. The first option is selected at first Enter Pick the selected option 1 to 8 Pick that option directly (a box has up to 8 options) Esc Skip the question; Labmill then asks in the chat instead

If none of the options fits, move to Other and type your own answer, then press Enter. Picking an option only answers the question: uploads, job submissions and downloads still ask for your approval separately.

items.title: In a sign-in box
items.text: Type the answer and press Enter. For the "trust this server?" question, use the arrow keys to choose Yes or No (No is the default). Esc cancels the sign-in.

items.title: The half-second pause
items.text:
When an approval, choice or sign-in box opens, Labmill ignores every key except Esc, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+D for half a second. This is a safety measure: if you were typing or pressing Enter just as the box appeared, those keys can't accidentally approve or pick something you hadn't seen yet. If a key seems to do nothing right after a box opens, press it again.

If the box doesn't fit in the window, enlarge the window. Until then only Esc and the quit keys work.

items.title: Privacy
items.text: The full privacy policy is at https://labmill.org/privacy/. This page tells what the client does.

items.title: What stays on your computer
items.text:
• Your files, until you approve an upload.
  • Your cluster password, two-factor codes and key passphrases. They are never written to disk.
  • Your Anthropic API key. Labmill reads it from the environment and never writes it to disk.
  • The job list, the causes of failed jobs and the log. They are kept in labmill.db and labmill.log on your computer.
  • Labmill has no telemetry. [CHECK: what the optional broker sees.]
  • Your Labmill program token, if you connect an account. It is kept in account.json, which only your user account can read.

items.title: What goes to Claude
items.text:
Labmill's assistant is Claude. Labmill sends to the Anthropic API with your own key (or to the broker, if you set one, or to the Labmill test relay, see below):

  • your messages;
  • the results of Labmill's actions: file names, folder sizes, short previews, job status, the end of a job log, and the output of commands on the cluster.

Labmill shows the assistant file names and metadata, and small samples only. It does not send whole data sets to Claude. Values that look like passwords, tokens or API keys are replaced by a placeholder before the assistant sees them.

Without your own ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, a client connected to your Labmill account uses the Labmill test relay (for invited testers): the same requests go through app.labmill.org to Anthropic, with Labmill's key. app.labmill.org does not store or log them; it keeps only token counts per day, for the limits. With your own key, the requests go to Anthropic directly and nothing goes through Labmill. That is the private choice.

items.title: What goes to your Labmill account
items.text: Nothing, unless you connect the client to your account at app.labmill.org. Then, for each job that ends after you connect, Labmill sends the cluster, the Slurm state, the times, the resources asked for, the partition and the software module names. It does not send job scripts, data files, program code, file, folder or job names, environment variables or log lines. See Connect the client to your Labmill account.

items.title: What goes to the cluster
items.text: Only what you approved: the files in the approved list, the job script, and commands that you approved (or that only read). Reads of files that hold keys or tokens ask first, because the content would go to Claude.

items.title: What Labmill does not read on your computer
items.text: Labmill refuses these on your own computer, even with approval: .ssh, .gnupg, .aws/credentials, .netrc, private keys (id_rsa, *.pem, *.key and similar), password files and shell histories. It does not choose hidden folders, system folders, ~/Library (macOS) or AppData (Windows).

items.title: What Labmill does not do
items.text:
• It needs no Labmill account. Connecting one is optional, and until you do, nothing goes to Labmill.
  • It has no shell on your computer. Claude uses fixed tools only.
  • It installs nothing on the cluster and leaves nothing running there.

items.title: Questions
items.text: Write to help@labmill.org.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
The desktop app has a Settings page where you can see and change everything Labmill keeps, without editing files. Open it with the gear button at the top right of the window, or choose Settings… in the tray menu (on a Mac: File → Settings…, Cmd+,). ← Back to chat (or Esc) takes you back to the chat.

The sections are listed on the left. With the keyboard, use the arrow keys (and Home or End) to move through the list; each section opens as you reach it, and Tab moves into it.

Settings never shows or stores a password, a sign-in code or a key. The one exception is the optional Labmill account section: it keeps the program token you paste there, in a file only you can read, and never shows it again. See Connect the client to your Labmill account.

items.title: Safety switches at a glance
items.text:
Switch Default What it does Run commands on the cluster without asking off Labmill runs commands on the cluster without showing them first. Approve everything automatically off Labmill approves every step. Secret-file reads, questions and logins still ask. Download results automatically off Labmill brings results of finished jobs to your computer. Notify me when a job ends on The desktop app shows a notification. Email me when a Slurm job ends off Labmill adds an email request to the job script.

Details for each switch are below. See also Privacy.

items.title: Institution
items.text: Shows the institution Labmill is set up for, and its documentation address (as text: copy it into your browser). Choose another institution from the list and click Save. Your clusters and connections stay as they are; the institution decides which help and skills Labmill uses.

items.title: A cluster at another institution
items.text: Labmill works with your own institution by default. If you name a cluster at another institution that Labmill has information for (for example "run this on the cluster at example.edu"), it asks you to approve adding that cluster. The approval is always shown, even with Approve everything automatically on. After you approve, the cluster is added to your list and can be used right away. The connection settings go into the same SSH settings file as your other clusters. You sign in to it with your own account there.

items.title: Clusters
items.text:
The clusters in clusters.yaml. Edit changes one, Add cluster adds one, Remove removes one (Labmill asks first).

  • Slurm clusters have a name, an SSH host (one of your SSH connections), an optional files host for transfers, an optional time zone (rarely needed) and the transfer method.
  • S3 staging (optional): bucket, prefix, region, AWS profile, endpoint and encryption. Keys never go here: Labmill uses the AWS profile you name. Leave all S3 fields empty for no S3 settings.

items.title: More clusters at your institution
items.text:
If your institution has gained a cluster since you first set up Labmill, the Clusters page lists it under More clusters at your institution (the section is hidden when nothing is missing). Add first shows what will be written: the SSH connection for the cluster's login host, the files that change, and your account name there (taken from your existing setup; change it if the cluster uses another account). If you already have an SSH entry for the same host, Labmill reuses it as it is and says so, with the account that entry names; Labmill signs in with that account, so if the account you type is a different one, Labmill refuses with a message instead of ignoring it (use that account, or change the existing entry first). Add cluster then adds it at the end of your list. A cluster you already have under another name is not offered again. Nothing is sent to or run on any cluster, and your existing clusters and connections stay as they are. You can also ask Labmill in the chat ("set up the cluster …"); it shows the same details for your approval, even with Approve everything automatically on. Labmill always tries the account name you already use at that institution (or at another cluster of it) first, and only asks for a different name if that sign-in is rejected; you can then tell it the other name in the chat. The terminal version lists these clusters in /settings and adds one when you ask in the chat.

Labmill checks your changes with the same rules it uses when it starts. If a value isn't valid, the message appears under that field and nothing is saved.

Before the first change, Labmill saves a copy of clusters.yaml next to it (clusters.yaml.labmill-backup-<date>-<time>). It never overwrites an older copy. Your comments in the file are kept.

items.title: SSH connections
items.text:
The connections Labmill uses: name, host name, user name, port and jump host.

  • Labmill's own connections (in ~/.ssh/config.d/labmill) can be edited, added and removed here. The name of an existing connection can't change, because clusters refer to it. A connection that a cluster uses can't be removed.
  • Your own entries in ~/.ssh/config are shown read-only. Labmill never changes them, and won't add a connection with the same name.
  • Each connection shows whether Labmill is logged in to it right now. Logins end by themselves 10 minutes after Labmill quits.

items.title: Folders
items.text: Your data folder (first) and code folder, the same ones as in the chat box's + menu: Choose…, Remove, or Use a recent folder. Only the folder names are kept; nothing is read or sent until you ask in the chat and approve.

items.title: App
items.text:
• Start Labmill in the tray when I log in: the same switch as in the tray menu. Off by default.
  • Show the one-time tips again: for example the note that Labmill keeps running in the tray when you close its window.
  • Notify me when a job ends: the desktop app shows a notification when one of your jobs ends. On by default.
  • Email me when a Slurm job ends: Labmill adds a request for an email when the job ends or fails to the Slurm script. The email goes to the default address of your institution. Off by default.

items.title: About and diagnostics
items.text:
Read-only: the version, the assistant's address (a broker address, or none when Labmill calls Anthropic directly), and where Labmill keeps its files (clusters, SSH settings, desktop app settings, job database, log).

  • Open logs folder opens the folder with Labmill's log and job database.
  • Copy diagnostics copies a short report for your site's support. The page shows exactly what is copied. It holds no passwords, keys, sign-in codes or user names.

items.title: Run commands on the cluster without asking
items.text: In the App section, Run commands on the cluster without asking is off by default. While it is off, Labmill runs plain reads on its own (for example listing your jobs or files) and shows you every other command, exactly as it will run, and waits for your OK. When you turn it on, Labmill runs those commands on your cluster account without showing them first. Reading a file that holds sign-in secrets, such as a private key or a token file, still asks first, because the content would go to Claude. Your cluster account's own permissions still decide what a command can do. The setting applies to the next command, and it is kept for the desktop app and the terminal alike.

items.title: Approve everything automatically
items.text:
In the App section, under Approvals, Approve everything automatically is off by default. The same checkbox is in the main chat window, next to Send. When it is on, Labmill approves every step for you, without showing it first and without letting you edit it: uploads, downloads, job submissions, cancellations and commands on the cluster. A banner above the chat says Auto-approve is on and has a Turn off button, and every step appears in the chat as Auto-approved: ..., so you can still see what was done.

Three things always ask, even when it is on:

  • Reading a file that holds sign-in secrets, such as a private key or a token file, because the content would go to Claude.
  • Questions from Labmill with a few answers to choose from.
  • Logins: your password and the two-factor push or code.

How it differs from "Run commands on the cluster without asking". That setting only covers commands on the cluster. Uploads, downloads and job submissions still show their approval screen. Approve everything automatically includes everything that setting does, and the other approval screens too. You can keep the narrower one on and the wider one off. Turn the wider one on only when you trust what you are asking for, because nobody checks each step. The setting applies to the next step.

items.title: Download results automatically
items.text:
In the App section, under Approvals, Download results automatically is off by default. The same checkbox is in the main chat window, next to Approve everything automatically. When it is on and a job you started completes, fails or runs out of time (not when you cancel it), Labmill downloads its results to your results folder, in the folder named after the job, and checks the files against the cluster. It asks nothing, because the files only come to your computer. The chat says what was downloaded and where, with an Open folder button.

It brings only what the job produced: files you uploaded, hidden or private-looking files (such as .netrc, .env or token files), environments and caches, and symbolic links are left out, and the chat says how many. It leaves results above 2 GB or 2000 files, or larger than your free disk space minus 10 %, for you to ask for, and says why. When you are not signed in, it tells you once and downloads at its next check after you sign in. When the download fails, it tells you and you can ask Labmill to fetch the results. A failed job stays marked as failed. Each job is downloaded automatically at most once, and only if it finishes while the setting is on. The setting applies to the next job that finishes, and it is kept for the desktop app and the terminal alike.

items.title: When changes take effect
items.text: Labmill reads clusters.yaml and the SSH settings when it starts. After you save a change, the page says so: quit labmill (tray menu → Quit Labmill) and open it again to use the new settings. Folders and the App settings, including Run commands on the cluster without asking and Approve everything automatically, take effect at once.

items.title: In the terminal
items.text: In the terminal interface, type /settings to see the same settings (without secrets) and where the files are. /settings also shows whether commands on the cluster run without asking. To change it from the terminal, add the line "runWithoutAsking": true (or false) to the desktop app settings file that /settings lists under Files (gui.json, in the same folder as clusters.yaml; create it as { "runWithoutAsking": true } if it is missing). A running desktop app may overwrite a hand edit with its own copy, so edit the file while the app is closed, or use the Settings page. Type /autoapprove on or /autoapprove off to change Approve everything automatically (/autoapprove alone shows it). Type /autodownload on or /autodownload off to change Download results automatically (/autodownload alone shows it; /settings shows both). The terminal's status line reads AUTO-APPROVE ON while it is on. The choice is saved in the same file as the desktop app's, so both use it. Editing is done in the desktop app, or in the files themselves.

items.title: Using the saved SSH settings in a terminal
items.text:
Labmill saves your cluster connection settings in the standard OpenSSH format. If you ever want to work on a cluster by hand, you can use the saved name, called an alias, in any terminal:

ssh bigcluster-login

The alias for each cluster is in ~/.config/labmill/clusters.yaml (the ssh_host entry) and in the file ~/.ssh/config.d/labmill. It carries your user name, the host, and any jump host, so you don't have to type them. If you already had your own SSH name for the same cluster, Labmill reused it and you keep using that.

On macOS and Linux, the settings also tell ssh to keep the login open for 10 minutes after you disconnect, so a second terminal window doesn't ask for your password and two-factor approval again. (These lines are left out on Windows, where the built-in OpenSSH doesn't support them.) The terminal's login is separate from Labmill's own, so you may be asked once more the first time.

Your password and two-factor approvals work exactly as they do for any cluster login. Labmill doesn't store them.

items.title: A terminal on the cluster from Labmill
items.text:
While Labmill is signed in to a cluster, you can open a terminal on its login node without a new password or approval:

labmill shell bigcluster

Use the cluster name from Labmill. To start in a folder on the cluster, add it: labmill shell bigcluster --dir /data/mygroup/project. Inside the terminal interface, type /shell bigcluster (also with --dir); Labmill steps aside, shows a short note, and comes back when you type exit. If Labmill is not signed in, it asks for your password and approval first, once. This works in a Windows console, Terminal.app and Linux terminals alike.

The terminal is yours: what you type and see there is not sent to the assistant or saved in the chat, and the assistant never uses it. Labmill only records in its log that a terminal was opened and closed on the cluster. Labmill keeps the sign-in open while the terminal is open.

items.title: If file transfers fail
items.text: If uploads or downloads fail with odd errors, check your login files on the cluster (for example ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile or ~/.cshrc). A file that prints text every time you log in, such as a greeting, echo lines or a module list, breaks file transfers. Move such lines so they only run for interactive logins, or remove them, and try again.

items.title: Labmill says it has no assistant
items.text: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set in the program's environment, and the client is not connected to a Labmill account. Set the key (or, if you are an invited tester, run labmill login), then start Labmill again. On Windows, set a user environment variable and open a new window. A desktop app started from the Start menu needs the variable set before you log in. [CHECK: how the desktop app on macOS finds the key when started from Finder.]

items.title: macOS or Windows blocks the program
items.text: The programs are not signed at first. See Install.

items.title: No two-factor push arrives
items.text:
• You may not be enrolled in two-factor sign-in. Labmill shows your institution's setup page when it knows it. Or ask your help desk.
  • Your phone may be offline.
  • The push may have been denied or have expired.

Fix the cause, then ask Labmill to try again.

items.title: The password is rejected
items.text: Labmill tries once and stops, because many clusters lock an account after repeated failures. Check or reset your password, then ask Labmill to try again.

items.title: "Still refusing connections"
items.text: The cluster shut the door for a short time after several sign-in tries. Wait a few minutes and start again.

items.title: The server identity changed
items.text: Labmill refuses to connect and tells you not to continue. This can mean that someone intercepts the connection. Contact your cluster support.

items.title: Uploads or downloads fail with odd errors
items.text: Check your login files on the cluster (~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.cshrc). A file that prints text at every login (a greeting, echo lines, a module list) breaks file transfers. Make such lines run only for interactive logins.

items.title: A file does not answer
items.text: A file in a cloud folder (for example OneDrive "files on demand") or on a network drive can stop answering. Labmill skips it after a few seconds and tells you which file. Make the file available offline and ask again.

items.title: A key press does nothing right after a box opens
items.text: Labmill ignores keys for half a second when an approval box opens. Press the key again. See the keyboard reference.

items.title: The window is too small for an approval
items.text: Enlarge the window. Until then only Esc (decline) works.

items.title: The tray icon is missing (Linux)
items.text: Your desktop may have no system tray. GNOME needs the AppIndicator extension. Without a tray, closing the window quits Labmill.

items.title: Labmill stops after many steps
items.text: After 80 steps in one go, Labmill stops so you can check in. Type continue.

items.title: My settings changes have no effect
items.text: Labmill reads clusters.yaml and the SSH settings when it starts. Quit Labmill from the tray menu and start it again.

items.title: Logs
items.text: The log is labmill.log in the folder of the job database (~/.local/state/labmill/ by default). In the desktop app, Settings > About and diagnostics > Open logs folder opens it. Copy diagnostics makes a short report without passwords, keys, codes or user names. Send it with your question to help@labmill.org.

items.title: Know-how updates
items.text: Labmill's knowledge about clusters (how to choose the software, how to fix common failures, what your institution's storage folders are) improves over time. When Labmill uses a relay service (a broker, see Starting Labmill), you don't have to install a new version of the app to get it. Without a broker, Labmill uses the know-how that came with the app.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
• While Labmill is open, it quietly asks the broker whether newer cluster know-how exists for your institution. This runs in the background and never delays your chat.
  • A newer set is downloaded and checked before it is kept: every file must match its published checksum. A set that fails the check is thrown away and Labmill keeps using what it has.
  • A downloaded set is used from the next start of labmill, never in the middle of a conversation, so the advice in a chat stays consistent.
  • When Labmill notices that newer know-how exists, it shows a one-line notice in the chat: "Updated cluster know-how is available; Labmill uses it from the next start."
  • If you are offline, or the service has nothing newer, Labmill uses the know-how that came with the app. Nothing breaks.
  • After you install a newer version of the app itself, the know-how that came with it is used until the next download.
  • You only ever receive the know-how for your own institution, plus the general parts.

items.title: Your own changes always win
items.text:
If you keep your own modified copies of the skills in Labmill's skills folder (~/.config/labmill/skills), those files are used instead of the downloaded or built-in ones. Labmill tells you once per session: "Using your own modified skills from ." Updates never overwrite your files.

If you also use the same skills in Claude Code, see the Claude Code page: those copies are separate and are updated by you.

items.title: Voice: "Hey Labmill"
items.text:
Planned, not yet available

Voice activation is a design for the desktop app on Windows and macOS. It isn't built yet. The text chat described in the rest of this guide is what exists today.

items.title: The idea
items.text:
You say "Hey Labmill" and the Labmill window comes to the front with the cursor in the chat box. Labmill then presses your computer's own dictation shortcut for you (Win+H on Windows, or the dictation shortcut you have set in System Settings on a Mac), so you can speak your request instead of typing it.

Dictation often mishears technical words, so Labmill will correct them ("S batch" becomes sbatch, folder and cluster names are matched to the real ones). It will show you the corrected text and wait for you to confirm before doing anything. If the request is still unclear, it asks. If dictation doesn't start or nothing is heard, Labmill retries once and then tells you what went wrong.

On a Mac, you would be asked once to allow the microphone, speech recognition and accessibility (needed to press the shortcut).

items.title: Privacy
items.text:
The listening for the phrase "Hey Labmill" is planned to stay on your device. Windows voice typing may use Microsoft's online speech service, and macOS Dictation runs on your device on Apple silicon for supported languages and may otherwise use Apple's service. The resulting text goes to Claude like any message you type. Every approval still applies.

Voice is not planned for the text-window version.
